Statistical inference

In this activity you will repeat the two types of resampling-based inference that are covered in the videos:

  1. permutation tests
  2. bootstrap samples

but using the all the Adelie penguins in the in the palmerpenguins data set.

Begin by loading the required packages

library("ggplot2")
library("withr")
library("infer")
library("dplyr")

Attaching package: 'dplyr'
The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag
The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library("palmerpenguins")

Next we will create a data frame containing just the Adelie penguins

adelie <- penguins |> 
  filter(species == "Adelie" & !is.na(sex) & !is.na(bill_length_mm))

Sexual dimorphism in Adelie penguins

In the following section you will investigate sexual dimorphism in the bill lengths of Adelie penguins using the entire data set of Adelie penguins.

Sexual dimorphism will be reflected in male Adeli penguins in the data set being drawn from a population of similar male Adelie penguins with a mean bill length that is different to that of the population of female Adelie penguins.

Hence our null hypothesis will be that

male and female Adelie penguins are drawn from populations with the same (equal) average bill length

Mathematically we would write this as

\text{H}_0: \mu_{\text{male}} = \mu_{\text{female}}

Our alternative hypothesis is that

male and female Adelie penguins are drawn from populations with different verage bill lengths

which we would write mathematically as

\text{H}_{\text{a}}: \mu_{\text{male}} \neq \mu_{\text{female}}\:.

We can reformulate these hypotheses in terms of a difference of means, with \text{H}_0 then being where the difference of means between the two sexes is equal to 0 (the means are not different), while text{H}_{\text{a}} implies that the difference of means is \neq 0:

We will assess these hypotheses using a permutation test and then add a confidence interval on the estimated difference in mean bill length between the two sexes using bootstrap resampling.

Permutation tests using infer

We start with a permutation test. For this we will use tools from the infer package that you loaded earlier.

The code needed to generate 1000 permutations of the original data is shown below

adelie_shuffled <- withr::with_seed(2,
  adelie |>
    specify(bill_length_mm ~ sex) |>
    hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
    generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute")
)

We use:

  • specify() to indicate to infer which is the response variable and which is the explanatory verariable. Here we are interested in variation in bill_length_mm due to sex so we specify that bill_length_mm is the response variable on the left of the ~ and sex is the explanatory variable which goes on the right of ~,
  • hypothesize() to indcate that our null hypothesis is one of independence, i.e. that there is no relationship between bill length and sex,
  • generate() to generate the 1000 permutations of the original data.
  • withr::with_seed() to set the random number generator to a known state.

For each permuted data set we need to compute the

  1. mean bill_length_mm for the males — \hat{\mu}_{\text{male}}
  2. mean bill_length_mm for the females — \hat{\mu}_{\text{female}}
  3. the difference of these two means: \hat{\mu}_{\text{male}} - \hat{\mu}_{\text{female}}

This difference of means will be our test statistic.

To do this we use the calculate() function:

adelie_null_distribution <- adelie_shuffled |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("male", "female"))
  • "diff in means" is how we tell infer that we want a difference of means test statistic,
  • order is used to set the order of operations in the difference. We set male before female so that positive values of the difference will indicate males are larger than females.

The ordering doesn’t matter so long as we are consistent throughout.

What is stored in adelie_null_distribution is know as the null distribution of the test statistic, or the sampling distribution of the difference of means under the null hypothesis.

We can plot the distribution using

adelie_null_distribution |>
  visualise(bins = 30)
Question

Describe the shape of the null distribution you generated. What distribution does this resemble?

Solution

The null distribution appears roughly bell-shaped, with a peak in the middle and approximate symmetry about this peak.

The distribution that this resembles is a Gaussian or Normal distribution.

We will now compute the observed value of the test statistic using the same pipeline as before, but without the hypothesize() and generate() steps

obs_diff_means <- adelie |>
  specify(bill_length_mm ~ sex) |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("male", "female"))

obs_diff_means
Response: bill_length_mm (numeric)
Explanatory: sex (factor)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
   stat
  <dbl>
1  3.13
Question

What does this number represent? Are male Adelie penguins larger on average in the sample than females?

Solution

In our sample, male Adelie penguins are 3.13mm larger than femal Adelie penguins.

We can shade the part of the distribution that is as extreme as or more extreme than the observed value of the test statistic

adelie_null_distribution |>
  visualise(bins = 30) +
    shade_p_value(obs_stat = obs_diff_means, direction = "both")

This is the p value region. We can compute a permutational p value using get_p_value()

adelie_null_distribution |>
  get_p_value(direction = "two-sided", obs_stat = obs_diff_means)
Warning: Please be cautious in reporting a p-value of 0. This result is an approximation
based on the number of `reps` chosen in the `generate()` step.
ℹ See `get_p_value()` (`?infer::get_p_value()`) for more information.
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  p_value
    <dbl>
1       0

The p value returned is equal to 0, which doesn’t make sense as we have at least one test statistic as extreme as the observed one; it is the observed value of the test statistic! Hence we would compute the p value in such cases to be

1 / 1001
[1] 0.000999001

Bootstrap confidence interval

The bootstrap can be used to generate confidence intervals on parameter estimates. A bootstrap sample is one where we draw a data set at ranodm from the observed data that is the same size as the observed data set, but we draw randomly with replacement.

For example, to draw a 1000 bootstrap samples for the male Adelie penguins and compute the mean bill length for each sample we would use:

male_boot <- adelie |>
  filter(sex == "male") |>
  specify(response = bill_length_mm) |>
  generate(
    reps = 1000,
    type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate("mean")

male_boot |>
  visualize()

We can compute statistics using the bootstrap distribution. FOr example, the mean and the median of the bootstrap sample are

male_boot |>
  summarise(mean = mean(stat), median = median(stat))
# A tibble: 1 × 2
   mean median
  <dbl>  <dbl>
1  40.4   40.4

We can generate a confidence interval using the percentile method. For a 95% percentile-based conifdence interval we compute the 0.25th and 0.975th quantiles of the bootstrap distribution and the endpoints of the enterval:

male_ci <- male_boot |>
  get_ci(type = "percentile", level = 0.95)

We can visuliase this interval using

male_boot |>
  visualize() +
  shade_ci(endpoints = male_ci)

As far as our main question goes, that of evidence for sexual dimorphism in Adelie penguins, we should create a bootstrap sample for the difference of means

boot_distn <- withr::with_seed(42,
  adelie |>
    specify(bill_length_mm ~ sex) |>
    generate(
      reps = 1000,
      type = "bootstrap") |>
    calculate(
      stat = "diff in means",
      order = c("male", "female"))
)

The main difference is that now we want the difference of means as the test statistic and we set the order as previously set.

We visualise the distribution using

boot_distn |>
  visualize()
Question

Does the boostrap distribution of the difference of means include 0? What does this tell us about sexual dimorphism in Adelie penguins?

Solution

No, 0 is not included in the bootstrap distribution of the difference of means. This suggests that male Adelie penguins are on average larger than females after accounting for sampling error.

We can compute the confidence interval using the percentile method using

pc_ci <- boot_distn |>
  get_ci(type = "percentile", level = 0.95)

pc_ci
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  lower_ci upper_ci
     <dbl>    <dbl>
1     2.47     3.88
Question

Repeat this analysis for the Chinstrap penguins. Is there evidence of sexual dimorphism in Chinstrap penguin bill lengths?

Question

Using the same ideas, instead of comparing males and females of the same species of penguin, test the hypothesis that the flipper length of Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins are drawn from populations with the same mean length. For this exercise choose one sex, either male or female penguins from both species.

Test your hypothesis with a permutation test and use the bootstrap to create a confidence on the difference of mean flipper lengths for your chosen sex of pengguin.
